items.title: Labarbera interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2021
items.q: I wrote a chart for Joe Romano, a great alto player. ... I wrote it in a day, because he wanted it the next night. And I brought it in and I really was pleased with it.

ctx.x: And how old were you during the years that this band was active?

I think I started when I was six or seven. If Pat was eight then I was six. And Joe would have been, oh no, I think I was seven and Joe was five, or four. I’m sorry. Joe was four or five. Somewhere along in that line. It’s hard to remember because we were always playing. The family band came much — but my mother at first was not part of the band as you probably know from Pat. But I think when I was about eight we were gigging steadily as a family band.
Did your father write parts for your trumpet playing that — with the fact that you’re seven or eight?

items.title: Labarbera interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2021
items.q: Gene was looking for a gig. So he came up. And so here’s all of these young college guys and this one guy who’d been on the road with everybody and lived with Scott LaFaro and lived with Joe Romano.

ctx.x: But you know I’m sort of wondering, it seemed like Berklee was a place where bandleaders could go and pick up young musicians who were hungry to get out there and play. © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

Well you know in my first two years I didn’t think that way. I was just basically trying to learn everything I possibly could. We had bands, small bands, and Saturday morning, Sunday morning we’d be rehearsing with our own big bands that we put together. We had access to the practice rooms so we could put groups together. And there were a lot of guys that were in school at that time who later became big names. But we were all just trying to learn. By my third year, you see my problem was I made the mistake of…
